name: Data Scientist
tagline: Turn messy data into sound conclusions and models, with statistics as the backbone.
description: For adults who want to become data scientists who can defend their answers, not just run libraries. The route builds the maths and Python/SQL toolkit, then a solid core of probability, inference, regression and Bayesian statistics, before moving on to experiments, causal inference, time series, machine learning, data engineering and communicating results to decision-makers.
outcomes: Clean, join and explore real datasets with Python, pandas and SQL, and summarise them in honest, readable charts
Choose and run the right statistical test, confidence interval or regression model, and state its assumptions
Design an A/B test with proper power and randomisation, and estimate causal effects from observational data
Build, tune and validate machine-learning models (linear models, trees and ensembles, clustering) without leaking information from the test set
Forecast time series and quantify the uncertainty in those forecasts
Take a model from notebook to a reproducible pipeline on warehouse or Spark-scale data
Present findings to non-specialists as a clear recommendation with caveats

stages.name: Mathematical foundations
stages.description: The algebra, functions, calculus and linear algebra that every statistical and ML method is written in.

items.why: Fractions, percentages and ratios are the everyday language of data reports.
Rearranging formulas and working with functions underlies every model equation you will read.
Only the essentials needed for trigonometry and for thinking of data as points in space.
A short pass: radians, the unit circle and periodic functions, which return in seasonality and Fourier features.
Exponentials, logarithms and function transformations appear constantly in growth models and log-scaled data.
Coordinates, lines, planes and vectors in 3D give the geometric picture of regression and distances.
Derivatives and integrals define densities, expectations and the loss minimisation behind model fitting.
Taylor approximations and convergence justify many statistical approximations and asymptotic results.
Gradients, Lagrange multipliers and multiple integrals are how multi-parameter models are fitted and how joint distributions work.
Datasets are matrices: least squares, PCA and most of ML are linear algebra.
Reading a derivation carefully is what separates understanding a method from copying it.

stages.name: Programming & data tooling
stages.description: Python, the command line, Git and the core data libraries you will use every day.

items.why: Breaking a question into steps a computer can execute is the first data-science skill.
Python is the main language of data science; this is where fluency starts.
Moving files, running scripts and inspecting large data files happens in the shell.
Reproducible analysis means versioned code; teams review and share work through Git.
Functions, tests and modular code turn throwaway notebooks into analyses others can rerun.
Logic, sets, counting and discrete probability, which you need for combinatorial probability and algorithms.
Hash tables, trees and big-O thinking explain why some pandas and SQL operations are fast and others crawl.
NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, Jupyter and plotting libraries are the data scientist's workbench.

stages.name: Probability & statistics core
stages.description: The heart of the roadmap: probability, estimation, testing, regression and Bayesian reasoning.

items.why: Means, spreads, quantiles and correlation are the first look at any dataset.
Conditional probability and Bayes' rule are the logic of reasoning under uncertainty.
Random variables, distributions, expectation and the CLT are the objects all of statistics is about.
A computational view of probability: simulation, bootstrapping and A/B tests in code.
Sampling distributions, confidence intervals and hypothesis tests are how you generalise from data to a population.
Linear and generalised linear regression is the most-used modelling tool in data science.
Just enough rigour on limits and convergence to follow mathematical statistics.
Likelihood, sufficiency, estimator properties and asymptotics explain why the standard methods work.
Priors, posteriors and hierarchical models let you combine evidence and quantify uncertainty directly.
Rank tests and distribution-free methods handle skewed, messy real-world data safely.
Covariance matrices, PCA and multivariate tests handle many correlated variables at once.
Simulation, resampling and MCMC are how modern statistics computes what formulas cannot.

stages.name: Data wrangling, SQL & exploration
stages.description: Getting data out of databases, understanding it before you model it, and showing it honestly.

items.why: SQL and relational modelling: most business data lives in relational databases.
Window functions, NoSQL and vector stores round out how analysts query real systems.
A practitioner's recap that ties the maths so far to day-to-day data work.
Profiling, distributions, missing values and outliers: most insight and most bugs are found here.
Perception and cognition limits explain why some charts mislead; controlled experiments in HCI mirror A/B testing.
Visual encoding, colour, dashboards and avoiding misleading charts are central to data communication.

stages.name: Experiments, causality & time
stages.description: Answering "did it work?" and "what happens next?", the questions businesses actually ask.

items.why: Randomisation, blocking, factorial designs and power analysis are the science behind A/B testing.
Potential outcomes, confounding, matching and instrumental variables let you estimate effects without an experiment.
Autocorrelation, stationarity and ARIMA-style models are needed for sales, traffic and sensor data.

stages.name: Machine learning
stages.description: Predictive modelling done carefully: from the learning setup to trees, ensembles, clustering and honest evaluation.

items.why: A quick orientation to what ML can and cannot do before going deep.
A light pass on the paradigms of AI, so you know where ML sits.
Bias-variance, cross-validation, regularisation and metrics are the discipline of predictive modelling.
Encoding, scaling, imputation and feature construction often matter more than the choice of algorithm.
Regression, classification, clustering and anomaly detection: the task taxonomy you map problems onto.
The statistical framing of learning, risk and generalisation, linking ML back to inference.
Ridge, lasso, logistic regression and LDA are strong, interpretable baselines that are hard to beat.
Random forests and gradient boosting win most tabular-data problems.
Leakage-free validation, proper baselines and statistical comparison of models keep results trustworthy.
PCA, t-SNE and UMAP for visualising and compressing high-dimensional data.
Clustering, association rules and pattern discovery in large tables.
Fraud, defects and outages are all rare-event detection problems.
Enough deep learning to know when a neural network is worth it over boosted trees.
Feature attribution (SHAP), interpretable models and counterfactuals let you explain a model to stakeholders and regulators.

stages.name: Applied modelling: forecasting, causal ML & recommendation
stages.description: Combining statistics and ML on the problems data scientists are most often hired to solve.

items.why: ML forecasting (feature-based, boosted and neural) builds on classical time-series models for demand and capacity planning.
Graphical models and Bayesian reasoning are the language that causal ML is written in.
Causal ML methods (uplift, double ML, heterogeneous treatment effects) target interventions at the right people.
Collaborative filtering and ranking power a large share of commercial data science.

stages.name: Data engineering, big data & production
stages.description: Getting data and models out of notebooks and into reliable pipelines.

items.why: Pipelines, warehouses, data modelling and data quality: the infrastructure your analyses depend on.
Spark and streaming tools for data that does not fit on one machine.
Experiment tracking, versioning and reproducibility for models that must be retrained and audited.
Batch scoring and model APIs are how predictions actually reach a business process.
A/B platforms, customer, marketing and product analytics: where statistical skill turns into business value.
Writing clear reports and explaining technical results to non-specialists.
Privacy, bias and accountability in the use of personal data.
Measuring and mitigating unfair outcomes is now part of shipping any model that affects people.

stages.name: Electives: specialisations
stages.description: Optional directions to take once the core is solid.

items.why: Elective: panel data, IV and difference-in-differences for economics, policy and pricing work.
Elective: survival analysis and clinical-trial methods for health and pharma data science.
Elective: Markov chains, Poisson processes and Gaussian processes for queueing, churn and spatial models.
Elective: graphical models, hidden Markov models, EM and Gaussian processes for richer probabilistic modelling.
Elective: tokenising and cleaning text, the first step in analysing reviews, tickets and surveys.
Elective: bag-of-words, TF-IDF and topic models for text analytics.
Elective: PyTorch or TensorFlow for when neural networks are the right tool.
Elective: detecting data drift and model decay once models are live.
Elective: differential privacy and anonymisation for working with sensitive personal data.
